title: One Order, Door to Door
performance: given a late order and its last tracking status, the viewer can name the station the order is stuck at, say what usually goes wrong there, and set a realistic expectation with the customer

audience.assumed_prior: has ordered online and seen tracking updates; has never seen a warehouse, hub or depot from the inside
audience.why: audience are employees in sales, service, finance or support whose work touches orders but not operations
audience.motivation: wants to answer 'where is my order' without guessing or overpromising
audience.context: desktop at work, with sound and captions, short break between tasks

strategy.name: concrete_first
strategy.rationale: the topic is a physical chain that is easy to see when one parcel moves through it; each station's idea lands only once the viewer has watched the order pass it (F1, F2)
strategy.signature_move: show the order arriving at the station, show what the station does to it, THEN name the station and the one way it can stall there

misconceptions.belief: tracking shows the parcel's live location the whole way
misconceptions.why_tempting: apps show a moving map near the end, so people assume it is live throughout

misconceptions.belief: if the website showed it in stock, the item is definitely on a shelf
misconceptions.why_tempting: the website and the warehouse feel like one system

misconceptions.belief: a late order means someone was careless
misconceptions.why_tempting: a delay feels like a mistake by a person

hook.sketch: An order placed in the evening, expected tomorrow, still not here; a customer asks you where it is. Where would you even look?

arc.promise: follow this one order through one connected world and you will know which station to look at, and why
arc.bridge_from_prior: start from what the viewer already sees: a click, a wait and a doorbell; then lift the lid on the stations in between (F1)

sections.goal: the viewer can explain what the order station checks and two reasons an order is held there
concepts: payment and fraud or address checks

sections.goal: the viewer can describe pick and pack and the warehouse's common failure points
the viewer can use the linehaul schedule to work out how much later a parcel arrives when it misses its departure or its label cannot be read
the viewer can use a tracking status to locate the station a parcel last passed on the last mile

arc.payoff: return to the opening order: its last scan names the station it is waiting at, and the viewer can now say where it is and what to tell the customer

practice_ladder.what: the one order passes every station, each stall narrated and shown on the map
a tracking trail with a long gap after 'at hub'; the viewer names the station before the narrator does
the opening order's last status is shown; the viewer decides where it is and what to say

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: So far: order, pick, pack, hub. Which hand-off has a fixed departure the parcel can miss?
The trail shows 'at hub' and then nothing for a long time. Which station do you look at first?
recall_moments.answer: the hub: the gap after its scan often points to a parcel waiting there, such as a missed linehaul or an unreadable label (F23, F15, F16)
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: 'it is lost on the road' - a gap between scans often means waiting at a station, not moving (F21, F23)

transfer_tasks: next time someone asks where an order is, read its last status, name the station it points to, and say what usually holds an order there before giving a date

persona.voice: a capable colleague who knows the operation, calm and practical
persona.delivery_notes: brisk on the journey, slower on the linehaul departure and the scan idea, warm on the check

gagne.attention: hook: the late order and the customer's question
gagne.objective: promise: know which station to look at
gagne.recall_prior: bridge from click, wait and doorbell
gagne.present: stations in the order the parcel meets them
gagne.practice: recall prompt after sec3; quiz after sec4
gagne.feedback: quiz answer with the tempting wrong reading explained
gagne.assess: payoff: the viewer places the opening order
gagne.transfer: transfer task: read the last status before answering

merrill.problem_centered: the late order is the running problem
merrill.activation: the everyday click to doorbell view
merrill.demonstration: the order shown at each station before it is named
merrill.application: the gap-in-the-trail quiz and the payoff
merrill.integration: transfer task in the viewer's next customer conversation

mayer.coherence: one order, one world; no side examples
mayer.signalling: the stalled station highlighted on the map, one at a time
mayer.redundancy: on screen only station names and status words; narration explains
mayer.contiguity: each station lights up as it is named
mayer.pre_training: the bridge names hand-off before the stations

arcs.attention: a customer asking where their order is
arcs.relevance: the question every customer-facing role gets
arcs.confidence: every station shown worked before the quiz
arcs.satisfaction: the viewer places the opening order
